subject: A serious mistake in model block

messages.author: f8a4136bfeaed71c
messages.subject: A serious mistake in model block
parts:
Hi all,

Suppose I have the following simple codes to model an ordinal variable with missing values. No covariates are considered here. As we know that the missing part will be treated as parameters in stan. That is why they cannot be specified in parameters and transformed parameters blocks. So to overcome, I specify they as follows:


model {

int Y[N];
int Ymis[NmisY];

for (i in 1: NobsY){
Y[indY[i]] = Yobs[i];
}

for (i in 1: NmisY){
Y[indY[NobsY+i]] = Ymis[i]+1; // This line
}

print(Y[indY[NobsY+1]])
print(Ymis[1])
print(Ymis[10])

  for (i in 1 : N){
Y[i] ~ ordered_logistic(0, cutpoint);
}
print(Y[indY[NobsY+10]])
}

However, I found a serious mistake that the missing values does not change from iteration to iteration. From the print, I wander why Ymis is alsways 0.

So I have several questions:

1. Why is it 0 instead of varying?
2. Where should we declare the missing part (Ymis) to be sure that they are parameters.
3. Is is correct that everything we specify in model block is just something intermediate and should not play a role of parameters?

Thank you so much for your answers!

Kind regards,
Tran.

P/S: Full codes including R script are in attachment.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A serious mistake in model block
parts:
You declare Ymis but you never define it (i.e., give it a value).
I'm not sure what you were expecting to happen.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A serious mistake in model block
parts:
On Thursday, October 27, 2016 at 1:23:44 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
You declare Ymis but you never define it (i.e., give it a value).
I'm not sure what you were expecting to happen.

I think he was expecting that by declaring but not defining an integer array in the model block he could work around the fact that integer arrays cannot be declared in the parameters block, which is the wrong intuition. The reason we cannot deal with integer unknowns has to do with the fact that the sampling algorithm does not support them, rather than the language. Also, integer arrays are initialized to zero rather than NaN, so there is no exception thrown.

For a model like this, you basically have to do what Gibbs samplers would call data augmentation, where you declare a continuous latent variable of length N in the parameters block that has a logistic likelihood. But the observed outcomes only, you can restrict that latent variable to be between cutpoints with a transformation (meaning you have to deal with a scalar Jacobian correction). Then you model the latent variable as a function of predictors and the sampling performance will probably be bad.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A serious mistake in model block
parts:
Hi Ben and Bob,

What I do expect, similar to Openbugs and JAGS,  is that when I specify

Y~distribution(parameters*predictor) (here I mean categorical distributions)

and when Y have missing values then the algorithm will used observed values to estimate the parameters and the missing values will be automatically generated from the distribution given the current parameters and predictors.

Thus, after convergence, we have both the parameters estimates and imputed values for the missing.

That I think we can do in the generated quantities block. However, in the case of sequential modeling, such as Y ~ X, and X~ Z (in the same codes, which can be done in OpenBUGS and JAGS), and in case both Y and X have missing values, then I would like to generate missing X inside the model block, because I can use imputed values immediately for the model Y ~ X. The problem here is that X is binary, and the missing as we have discussed cannot be a parameter.

As you have said that use latent probably bad so I am wandering which is a better solution here.

Thank you for your time,

Tran.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A serious mistake in model block
parts:
On Friday, October 28, 2016 at 3:42:13 AM UTC-4, Dung Tran wrote:
What I do expect, similar to Openbugs and JAGS,  is that when I specify

Y~distribution(parameters*predictor) (here I mean categorical distributions)

and when Y have missing values then the algorithm will used observed values to estimate the parameters and the missing values will be automatically generated from the distribution given the current parameters and predictors.

You are expecting the wrong thing. There is an appendix in the Stan manual that explains most of the differences between the Stan language and the BUGS language. This particular mistake is common and could be avoided if you utilize the newer syntax

target += ordered_logistic_lpmf(y[i] | predictors[i] * parameters, cutpoints);

which makes it more explicit that all you are doing is adding the log-likelihood of the data to the target keyword (which is originally zero).

y[i] ~ ordered_logistic(predictors[i] * parameters, cutpoints);

implicitly does the same thing.

If some of the data are missing, then y needs to be the union of y_obs and y_miss in order to evaluate the so-called complete-data log-likelihood. However, when y_miss is discrete, HMC cannot proceed because you cannot differentiate the log-posterior with respect to an integer.
As you have said that use latent probably bad so I am wandering which is a better solution here.

There is no alternative. In parameters, declare both y_star_obs and y_star_miss as vectors or real arrays. Then transform y_star_obs[i] to be between the two cutpoints that pertain to the observed value of y_obs[i], making sure to handle the Jacobian adjustment. Combine that with the unrestricted values from y_star_miss to form y_star_complete and y_star_complete[i] is distributed standard logistic with expectation predictors[i] * parameters.

Ben
